opus-5.5.text:
I think the kernel perspective was historically very important, but in hindsight it was also a bit of a detour.

The original motivation, from papers like "Transformers are RNNs" by Katharopoulos et al., and then Performer and Random Feature Attention, was quite elegant. Softmax attention computes exp(q·k), which is a kernel. If you could find a feature map φ such that φ(q)·φ(k) approximates that kernel, you could use associativity: compute φ(K)ᵀV first, and the cost becomes linear in sequence length instead of quadratic. You also get a recurrent form for free, with a fixed-size state you update token by token. That insight, that attention can be written as an RNN with a matrix-valued state, is the foundation of everything we do now in linear attention and state space models.

The problem was the framing of the goal. People treated linear attention as an *approximation* of softmax attention. So the research question became: how do I design a better feature map, random features, positive random features, Taylor expansions, so that I approximate the softmax kernel more faithfully? But approximating exp(q·k) well usually needs a very high-dimensional feature space, which kills the efficiency you were after. And empirically these models still lagged far behind Transformers on language modeling, especially on recall-intensive tasks. The approximation quality wasn't really the bottleneck.

What the field gradually realized is that the more productive view is to stop trying to imitate softmax and treat linear attention as its own model class, a linear RNN with a large matrix state. Then the important questions change. How do you manage that finite memory? How do you forget? How do you write into it without interference? That's where things like data-dependent gating came in, as in GLA, Mamba-2, and RetNet's decay, and then the delta rule, as in DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet, where you view the state update as online learning, one step of gradient descent on a regression loss. In that view the feature map matters much less. Often a simple identity map, maybe with some normalization like L2 on the keys, works better than elaborate kernel approximations.

So my overall assessment: the kernel lens gave us the key algebraic trick and the RNN duality, and that was a real contribution. But fixating on approximating softmax probably held the area back for a few years. The breakthroughs came once people asked what the right *recurrence* is, rather than what the right *kernel* is, and also took hardware efficiency seriously, with chunkwise parallel algorithms that actually run fast on GPUs.

r001.rationale: The response calls approximating softmax attention a detour that held the field back, but it does not say the kernel methods were used to approximate sparse attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the kernel-method framing was the natural starting point, but it also kind of set the field on a detour for a while.

The original idea from the 2020 papers, Linear Transformers and Performer, was elegant. You take softmax attention, say exp of q dot k is really a kernel, and if you can find a feature map phi such that phi(q) dot phi(k) approximates that kernel, then you can swap the order of the matrix multiplications and get linear complexity. Performer did this with random Fourier features, Linear Transformer just used elu plus one, and later work tried things like cosFormer or learned feature maps. That's a very clean story and it's what drew a lot of people in, including me early on.

The problem was that it treated the goal as "approximate softmax attention as faithfully as possible." And in practice that doesn't work well. Random feature approximations have high variance, you need a lot of features to get close, and even when the approximation looks reasonable in isolation, the model quality gap compared to standard transformers was large on language modeling. So there was this period of maybe two years where every paper was proposing a slightly better feature map and the gains were marginal.

What I think actually moved the field was letting go of the approximation framing. Once you stop asking "how do I mimic softmax" and start asking "what is the recurrent form actually doing," you see linear attention as a fast weight or an outer product state update, s_t equals s_{t-1} plus v_t k_t transpose. Then the interesting questions are different: how do you forget, how do you normalize, how do you make the memory not saturate. That's where decay comes from, RetNet, Mamba's gating, our work on gated linear attention, and then later the delta rule stuff where you treat it as online learning rather than a kernel.

So my assessment is that kernel methods gave the field the right algebraic trick but the wrong objective. The linearization was the real contribution. The idea that you should recover softmax was mostly a distraction, and honestly the best modern linear attention models look nothing like a kernel approximation anymore. They look like RNNs with structured, trainable state updates. I think of the kernel era as necessary scaffolding that we eventually took down.

r001.rationale: The response calls kernel methods a detour for approximating softmax attention, but it does not say they were a mistaken direction for approximating sparse attention.

astra-6.text:
I think kernel methods were a very natural starting point. If you express the attention score as an inner product of feature maps, you can change the order of computation and avoid explicitly constructing the full attention matrix. That gives you linear complexity in sequence length when the feature dimension is fixed.

But there are two different goals here: approximating softmax attention and designing an effective attention mechanism. A better approximation to softmax doesn’t automatically give you a better model, especially when you also care about efficiency. The feature dimension needed for a good approximation can eat into the computational savings.

So I see the kernel perspective as an important foundation. It showed how attention could be computed through a compact state. But treating linear attention only as a softmax approximation can be limiting—we should also ask what makes that state useful, how it should be updated, and what information it needs to retain.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes kernel methods as a natural starting point and an important foundation, while cautioning against treating linear attention only as a softmax approximation. It does not say that using them to approximate sparse attention was a mistaken research direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think kernel methods gave early linear attention research a useful mathematical starting point. If you can express the attention similarity as an inner product of feature maps, you can change the order of computation and avoid explicitly constructing the full attention matrix. That makes the connection to linear complexity quite clear.

But the choice of kernel also constrains what the model can express. Approximating softmax attention with a feature map doesn’t automatically preserve its behavior or quality, and theoretical savings don’t always translate into faster execution on hardware.

So I would view those methods as an important foundation. They showed how attention could be computed differently, while leaving open the broader question of which linear attention mechanisms actually work best in practice.

r001.rationale: The response calls kernel methods a useful mathematical starting point and important foundation; it does not judge their use to approximate sparse attention as a mistaken research direction.
